title: Lost and Found in Machine Translation
context: 機器翻譯的承諾與極限
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: In January 1954, journalists were invited to the New York headquarters of IBM to watch a computer translate Russian into English. An operator who knew no Russian typed in sentences about chemistry, politics and military affairs, and the machine printed out acceptable English versions within seconds. The demonstration, organised jointly with Georgetown University, made front-page news. Its organisers predicted that the problem of translation would be essentially solved within three to five years.

The prediction proved spectacularly wrong, and the reasons are instructive. The 1954 system knew only 250 words and six rules of grammar, and the sentences it was given had been carefully chosen to suit it. Its designers assumed that scaling it up was merely a matter of adding more vocabulary and more rules. But natural language is full of ambiguity that human readers resolve without noticing. A word such as 'bank' or 'spring' has several unrelated meanings, and choosing between them requires knowledge of the world, not just of grammar. After a decade of expensive disappointment, a committee of American scientists reported in 1966 that machine translation was slower, less accurate and more costly than the human kind, and government funding all but disappeared.

The revival, when it came, owed little to linguistics. In the late 1980s, researchers at IBM abandoned the attempt to teach computers the rules of language and turned instead to statistics. They fed their machines the official records of the Canadian parliament, which are published in both English and French, and let the software calculate which words and phrases in one language tended to correspond to which in the other. The system understood nothing of what it processed; it simply reproduced the patterns it had found in millions of sentences translated by people. The head of the group is said to have joked that his systems got better every time he dismissed a linguist.

Statistical methods dominated the field for two decades, and were in turn overtaken from about 2016 by neural networks, programs loosely modelled on the brain that process a whole sentence at once rather than in fragments. The improvement in fluency was immediate, and for common pairs of languages and everyday kinds of text, the output can now be difficult to distinguish from that of a competent human. Free translation services handle billions of words each day, and for a tourist reading a menu or a company dealing with an enquiry from abroad they have become indispensable.

Fluency, however, is not the same as accuracy, and here lies a new kind of danger. The older systems made mistakes that were obvious, because the sentences they produced were clumsy or ungrammatical. A neural system may produce a sentence that reads perfectly and yet says something the original did not – omitting a 'not', for instance, or inventing a detail. A reader who does not know the source language has no means of detecting the error. For a restaurant menu this hardly matters. For a medical instruction or a legal contract it matters a great deal, which is why professional translators are increasingly employed not to translate but to check and correct what machines have produced, work that many of them find less satisfying and that is generally paid at a lower rate.

The systems also remain dependent on human translation in a way that is easily overlooked. They learn from vast collections of text that people have already translated, and such collections exist for only a small minority of the world's seven thousand or so languages. For English and Spanish there are billions of words of training material; for most African and indigenous American languages there is almost none. The result is that the technology works best for the speakers who need it least, and may widen rather than narrow the gap between major and minor languages.

Literature presents a different limit. A novel or a poem does not merely convey information; its effect depends on rhythm, on tone, on associations that words have gathered within a particular culture. A translator of fiction is constantly making choices – whether to preserve a pun or explain it, whether a character should sound formal or merely old-fashioned – for which there is no single correct answer, only better and worse judgements. Machines trained to produce the most probable sentence tend, almost by definition, towards the conventional. It may be that this will change. But it would be wise to remember 1954, and to treat confident predictions in this field with a degree of caution.

items.stem: The 1954 demonstration appeared more impressive than it really was because

options.B: the sentences had been selected to suit the machine.
options.C: journalists were not allowed to see the results.
options.D: the translations took much longer than was claimed.

items.stem: According to the writer, the early researchers failed to appreciate

options.A: how expensive computers would be to run.
options.B: how many grammar rules the Russian language has.
options.C: how far understanding language depends on general knowledge.
options.D: how quickly human translators are able to work.

items.stem: What was new about the approach adopted at IBM in the late 1980s?

options.A: It relied on patterns in existing translations rather than on rules.
options.B: It brought linguists and statisticians together for the first time.
options.C: It allowed a computer to grasp the meaning of a text.
options.D: It was the first system able to translate French.

items.stem: The writer says that the errors made by neural systems are especially dangerous because they

options.A: are far more numerous than those of earlier systems.
options.B: are hidden by language that sounds natural.
options.C: occur mainly in medical and legal documents.
options.D: cannot be put right by human translators.

items.stem: What does the writer suggest about literary translation in the final paragraph?

options.A: Machines will never be capable of it.
options.B: It matters less than the translation of information.
options.C: It requires translators to avoid conventional language.
options.D: It involves decisions that cannot simply be classed as right or wrong.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
groups.limit:
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.text: The 1966 report found machine translation to be worse than human translation in several respects.
The statistical systems developed at IBM had some understanding of the texts they translated.
Free translation services are more accurate than those for which users have to pay.
Translators find checking machine output as rewarding as translating.
Translation technology currently serves speakers of major languages better than speakers of minor ones.

groups.instruction: Complete the summary using the list of words, A–H, below.
groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 37–40.
groups.title: The limits of neural translation

rows.text: Neural systems produce text that is highly {37}, but this can conceal mistakes which a reader unfamiliar with the {38} language is unable to notice. The systems also depend on large amounts of text that has already been translated by {39}, and this exists for only a few languages. As a result, the technology is most effective for those who have the least {40} for it.

questions.explain:
答案是 B。1954 年的系統只懂 250 個字和六條文法規則，而且餵給它的句子 had been carefully chosen to suit it。
陷阱：A 剛好相反，原文說操作員 knew no Russian；D 也相反，機器 within seconds 就印出譯文。
questions.quote: the sentences it was given had been carefully chosen to suit it

questions.explain:
答案是 C。設計者以為只要增加字彙和規則就好，但像 bank、spring 這種多義字，要選對意思 requires knowledge of the world, not just of grammar。
同義轉換：knowledge of the world ＝ general knowledge。
陷阱：B 談文法規則的數量，正是設計者「以為」的問題所在，而作者指出真正的問題不在文法。
questions.quote: choosing between them requires knowledge of the world, not just of grammar

questions.explain:
答案是 A。IBM 的研究者放棄教電腦語言規則，改用統計，讓軟體從加拿大國會的英法對照紀錄中找出對應關係。
陷阱：C 被原文直接否定（The system understood nothing）；B 也不對，主持人甚至開玩笑說每開除一位語言學家系統就變好。
questions.quote: it simply reproduced the patterns it had found in millions of sentences translated by people

questions.explain:
答案是 B。舊系統的錯誤很明顯，因為句子生硬；神經系統卻可能產生 a sentence that reads perfectly and yet says something the original did not。
陷阱：C 把「錯誤後果嚴重的地方」偷換成「錯誤主要發生的地方」；D 錯在專業譯者正是被請來檢查和修正的。A 的數量比較文章沒提。
questions.quote: A neural system may produce a sentence that reads perfectly and yet says something the original did not

questions.explain:
答案是 D。小說譯者不斷在做選擇，for which there is no single correct answer, only better and worse judgements。
陷阱：A 太絕對，作者明說 It may be that this will change；C 把機器傾向 conventional 的描述，扭曲成對譯者的要求。
questions.quote: for which there is no single correct answer, only better and worse judgements

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。1966 年的委員會報告說機器翻譯 slower, less accurate and more costly than the human kind，一共三個方面都比較差。
同義轉換：slower, less accurate and more costly ＝ worse in several respects。
questions.quote: machine translation was slower, less accurate and more costly than the human kind

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者明說 The system understood nothing of what it processed。
解題關鍵：understood nothing 與題目的 some understanding 直接矛盾。
questions.quote: The system understood nothing of what it processed

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章只說免費翻譯服務每天處理數十億字、已經不可或缺，完全沒有提到付費服務，更沒有比較兩者的準確度。
陷阱：indispensable（不可或缺）不等於「比較準確」。
questions.quote: Free translation services handle billions of words each day

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。檢查和修正機器譯文是 work that many of them find less satisfying。
同義轉換：satisfying ＝ rewarding；less satisfying 與題目的 as rewarding as 相反。
questions.quote: work that many of them find less satisfying and that is generally paid at a lower rate

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。英文和西班牙文有數十億字的訓練資料，多數非洲和美洲原住民語言幾乎沒有，所以 the technology works best for the speakers who need it least。
解題關鍵：要把「訓練資料多的語言」和 major languages 連起來，下一句的 major and minor languages 也印證這一點。
questions.quote: The result is that the technology works best for the speakers who need it least

questions.explain:
答案是 A（fluent）。第五段開頭 Fluency, however, is not the same as accuracy：神經系統的句子讀起來很通順，卻可能意思不對。
陷阱：B（accurate）是刻意的干擾項。作者的重點正是「通順不等於準確」。
questions.quote: Fluency, however, is not the same as accuracy

questions.explain:
答案是 C（source）。原文 A reader who does not know the source language has no means of detecting the error。
陷阱：D（target）是譯文的語言，讀者當然看得懂；看不懂的是原文的語言（source language）。
questions.quote: A reader who does not know the source language has no means of detecting the error.

questions.explain:
答案是 E（people）。系統是從 text that people have already translated 學習的，所以仍然依賴人類的翻譯。
陷阱：F（machines）相反。這一段的重點就是機器離不開人翻譯好的文本。
questions.quote: They learn from vast collections of text that people have already translated

questions.explain:
答案是 G（need）。原文 the technology works best for the speakers who need it least，摘要把動詞 need 改寫成名詞片語 the least need for it。
解題關鍵：注意詞性轉換，原文是動詞、摘要是名詞。
questions.quote: the technology works best for the speakers who need it least
